title: Stats Resources
text:
Statistics Made Simple by Brad R. Fulton, PhD. Brad is a professor of social policy with decades of experience teaching statistics. He provides introductory-level (think 2nd year undergraduate student) lectures on basic concepts with limited math and formulas. As the title says, he aims to make statistics simple!
Quantitude by Greg Hancock, PhD and Patrick Curran, PhD. Greg is a statistician in the field of education and Patrick is a statistician in the field of psychology. They provide intermediate-level (think 2nd year graduate student) episodes on “all things quantitative”, from linear regression to structural equation modeling to philosophy of science, through explanation, discussion, and “grousing”. They provide an exemplar of the “modeling” approach to statistics in the social sciences.

title: Stats Resources
text:
Books


Applied Multiple Regression/Correlation Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (third edition) by Jacob Cohen, Patricia Cohen, Stephen G. West, and Leona S. Aiken. Still a great introduction to the General Linear Model (aka Linear regression, correlation, ANOVA, and t-tests), even though its an older text (originally written in 1975 and modified in 1983 & 2003). I have heard it referred to as the “Regression Bible” due to its comprehensive nature. Written for social science researchers and not statisticians, it provides an intermediate-level (think 2nd year graduate student) coverage of the foundation of applied statistics.
Introduction to Mediation, Moderation, and Conditional Process Analysis: A Regression-Based Approach (third edition) by Andrew F. Hayes, PhD. Andrew Hayes is the author of the very popular PROCESS macros for conducting mediation in SPSS, SAS, Stata, and R. Although other regression books cover moderation (aka interactions), his arguably does the best job of covering mediation and moderated mediation… and mediated moderation… etc.
Principles and Practice of Structural Equation Modeling (fifth edition) by Rex B. Kline, PhD. Rex has taught statistics courses to psychology graduate students for years and has continued to improve his seminal book on SEM with each subsequent edition. I recommend having a solid foundation in the multiple regression (see above) before reading it. Part of the Methodology in the Social Sciences Series, which has several other excellent books.

title: Stats Resources
text:
Videos


StatQuest YouTube channel by Josh Starmer. He has 5 to 30 minute videos on a wide range of statistical concepts and analyses. Some cover basic topics like standard error and linear regression while others cover more advanced topics such as Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Random Forests. Either way, he breaks statistics into bite site pieces so its digetable to non-statisticians. His videos have millions of views, perhaps because he embraces his nerdiness through song.
TidyTuesday screencasts of David Robinson, a top data scientist, using R and the tidyverse on publicly available data. What’s great about these videos is that they are not planned out ahead of time and polished like a formal lecture. Instead, they are videos of David analyzing real data in real time to show how he codes and thinks in R with the tidyverse. Hadley Wickham, lead author of the tidyverse, did one of these as well in honor of his love for cocktails, but David has dozens and dozens of them. (Also thank you to whoever took the time to organize these and post these all online!)

About me: David Disabato, PhD
I am a Biostatistics master’s student and Psychological Scientist. I am currently pursuing a career change from psychology to statistics. During my 20s, I received my PhD in Clinical Psychology from George Mason University outside Washington, DC. I received training in both scientific research and clinical practice. Over the past 4 years, I was an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Baldwin Wallace University in Berea, OH. Although I enjoy research and psychology, I realized being a college professor was not for me. I decided to pursue an alternative career in the two things I am most passionate about: stats and therapy. Statistics was always my favorite part about the research process, and I received a concentration in Quantitative Psychology during my doctoral training. I have become interested in the health sciences in general, which led me to the biostatistics master’s program at Case Western Reserve University’s School of Medicine. I am really enjoying the program as I learn more advanced statistics, probability theory, health care analytics, and R programming. While re-training in biostatistics, I am continuing my passion for therapy by providing individual psychotherapy part-time. Please visit the Royalton Psychological Associates group practice website for information about my therapy practice.
I have a strong foundation in statistics for the social sciences. I have taken university courses or in-person workshops (e.g., Stats Camp) on the following analyses: ANOVAs & t-tests, Moderation and Mediation, Generalized Linear Models (e.g., logistic regression), Multiple Imputation (for missing data), Linear Mixed-Effects Models (aka Multi-Level Models), Exploratory and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (EFA & CFA), Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), Latent Profile Analysis (LPA), Latent Growth Mixture Modeling (LGMM), and Multilevel Structural Equation Modeling (MSEM). Throughout my career, I provided informal statistical consulting to my colleagues in psychology. This allowed me opportunities to publish papers using the above statistical analyses. Please see my Publications page for a list of peer reviewed scholarly articles organized by statistical analysis. You will see the content areas range within psychology from well-being/quality of life, emotional disorders (e.g., depression, social anxiety), health behaviors (e.g., nutritious eating, exercise), character strengths (e.g., grit, gratitude, curiosity), marriage and divorce, criminal thinking, suicide prevention, help-seeking, to spirituality (e.g., meaning in life, religiosity). Additionally, I have been involved in data collection for a number of longitudinal cohort studies that spanned multiple years.
My favorite statistical software is R through the use of RStudio. I was first introduced to R in 2012 by my statistics professor, Patrick McKnight, PhD. Initially trained in SPSS, I struggled to learn R at first. I remember taking a coursera class in R by the statistician Roger Peng, PhD to get my footing. However, after getting past the growing pains (see The R Inferno), I loved how powerful and flexible R was. I have not looked back since as R is my go to statistical software. I have authored two R packages and hope to create more in the future. Please see my R packages page for details and links.
Although almost anything you could ever want to know is on the internet, it is not always easy to find. Over the years, I have collated a list of helpful statistics and data analysis resources. I included them on my website in case they are of use to others (and as any good programmer knows, future me). Please see my Stats Resources page for these resources.
In the near future, I will be starting up a statistical consulting company. Feel free to email me at david.disabato@case.edu if you are interested in my consulting services. Please see my CV page to download my Curriculum Vitae.

title: R packages
text: Below is information on my two R packages available on CRAN. R is open-source statistical software used for data analysis all over the world (https://www.r-project.org/). In addition to its base packages, R allows for add-on packages - written by users like me (or you!) - to enhance its software capabilities. There are currently over 25,000 R packages available on CRAN, written by data analysts from dozens of countries.

title: R packages
text:
str2str

Convert R Objects from One Structure to Another

Offers a suite of functions for converting to and from (atomic) vectors, matrices, data.frames, and (3D+) arrays as well as lists of these objects. It is an alternative to the base R as..() functions (e.g., as.data.frame.array()) that provides more useful and/or flexible restructuring of R objects. To do so, it only works with common structuring of R objects (e.g., data.frames with only atomic vector columns).

str2str CRAN webpage

title: R packages
text:
quest

Prepare Questionnaire Data for Analysis

Offers a suite of functions to prepare questionnaire data for analysis (perhaps other types of data as well). By data preparation, I mean data analytic tasks to get your raw data ready for statistical modeling (e.g., regression). There are functions to investigate missing data, reshape data, validate responses, recode variables, score questionnaires, center variables, aggregate by groups, shift scores (i.e., leads or lags), etc. It provides functions for both single level and multilevel (i.e., grouped) data.
